name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5

lead: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is a small four-amino-acid peptide used as an ingredient in eye-area cosmetics, usually under the trade name Eyeseryl. People use products containing it because the under-eye area is where puffiness and swollen-looking lower lids show most, and a smoother, flatter lower lid can make a face look more rested.

Ingredient suppliers describe it as acting on fluid retention and on glycation-related changes in the thin skin around the eyes. Published research specific to the ingredient is sparse; the human data that exist usually come from supplier-run studies of finished creams, and the lab literature mostly covers peptide mixtures in general.

paras: It is applied topically as part of an eye cream, gel or serum, typically once or twice daily around the orbital bone, often alongside caffeine, hyaluronic acid or other peptides. Users generally report judging results over several weeks, and many routines combine it with sunscreen and sleep habits aimed at the same puffy-eye goal.

As a topical cosmetic peptide it is generally considered a low-irritation ingredient, though any product around the eyes can sting or cause contact reactions in sensitive people, and fragrance or other ingredients in the finished formula are often the cause. Eye bags that appear suddenly or persist can have medical causes, which clinicians evaluate separately.

Marketed to limit fluid retention and glycation in periorbital skin
angle.text: It is used topically around the eyes to reduce the look of puffiness and bags. The appearance benefit is the one described by suppliers and brands: a smoother, more rested under-eye contour.

lead: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5, sold by ingredient suppliers as Eyeseryl, is a synthetic four-amino-acid peptide used in cosmetic eye creams and gels. It is marketed for the under-eye area, where swelling, bags and a tired look are among the most common appearance concerns.

People use products containing it to try to reduce the look of puffiness, so that the lower lid looks flatter and the eye area looks more rested. Suppliers describe two lines of action: limiting fluid build-up in the thin periorbital tissue and slowing glycation-related changes to skin proteins.

The scientific literature on cosmetic peptides is large in general, but studies naming this particular peptide are few. One laboratory study examined five peptide mixtures used in cosmetics on human skin fibroblasts stressed with hydrogen peroxide, looking at markers of senescence and extracellular-matrix protection.[1]

paras: Acetyl tetrapeptide-5 is an acetylated chain of four amino acids made for cosmetic use. It is supplied to brands as a raw ingredient and listed on labels by its INCI name, and it is most often found in products aimed at the eye contour, such as gels, roll-on serums and creams.
Formulators usually pair it with other eye-area actives, including caffeine, hyaluronic acid and other peptides, so the effect of the peptide alone is hard to separate in finished products.

Supplier literature describes the peptide as reducing the accumulation of fluid in the lower-lid tissue and counteracting glycation, in which sugars attach to collagen and other proteins and alter skin quality. These are manufacturer claims; independent confirmation in published human studies has not been located for this specific ingredient.

Under-eye puffiness and eye bags are a recurring topic in appearance communities because the periorbital region strongly affects perceived tiredness and age. Peptide eye creams are one of several topical options people discuss, next to caffeine products, cold compresses, sleep and salt-intake changes, and in-office procedures.

No studies found for acetyl tetrapeptide-5 specifically in peer-reviewed human trials. Related laboratory work has tested mixtures of cosmetic peptides on cultured human skin fibroblasts, reporting protective and anti-aging effects in that cell model.[1]
